claim: Translation of the genetic code by the ribosome is hypothesized to be exceptionally sensitive to small chemical changes to its template mRNA.
source: Similar to DNA replication, translation of the genetic code by the ribosome is hypothesized to be exceptionally sensitive to small chemical changes to its template mRNA.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the abstract without direct experimental support in the quoted text.

claim: The addition of common alkylating agents to growing cultures of Escherichia coli leads to the accumulation of several adducts within RNA, including N(1)-methyladenosine (m1A).
source: Here we show that the addition of common alkylating agents to growing cultures of Escherichia coli leads to the accumulation of several adducts within RNA, including N(1)-methyladenosine (m1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The introduction of m1A to model mRNAs reduces the rate of peptide bond formation by three orders of magnitude in a well-defined in vitro system.
source: As expected, the introduction of m1A to model mRNAs was found to reduce the rate of peptide bond formation by three orders of magnitude in a well-defined in vitro system.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Alkylative stress is likely to stall translation in vivo and necessitates the activation of ribosome-rescue pathways.
source: These observations suggest that alkylative stress is likely to stall translation in vivo and necessitates the activation of ribosome-rescue pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro data showing reduced peptide bond formation.

claim: The addition of alkylation agents robustly activates the transfer-messenger RNA system, even when transcription is inhibited.
source: Indeed, the addition of alkylation agents was found to robustly activate the transfer-messenger RNA system, even when transcription was inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bacteria carefully monitor the chemical integrity of their mRNA and evolved rescue pathways to cope with its effect on translation.
source: Our findings suggest that bacteria carefully monitor the chemical integrity of their mRNA and they evolved rescue pathways to cope with its effect on translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed activation of tmRNA in response to alkylation damage.

claim: RNA is more susceptible to chemical insults than DNA, in part due to its exposed Watson-Crick (WC) hydrogen-bonding interface.
source: RNA is more susceptible to chemical insults than DNA, in part due to its exposed Watson-Crick (WC) hydrogen-bonding interface (Hofer et al., 2005; Wyatt and Pittman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The integrity of the WC face is paramount during codon recognition of the tRNA selection process.
source: Notably, the integrity of the WC face is paramount during codon recognition of the tRNA selection process, during which the three nucleotides of the codon base pair with those of the anticodon of the tRNA (Zaher and Green, 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge about translation.

claim: Changes that disrupt the ability of the mRNA to properly base pair with the cognate tRNA are highly likely to reduce translational speed and fidelity.
source: Changes that disrupt the ability of the mRNA to properly base pair with the cognate tRNA are then highly likely to reduce translational speed and fidelity (Simms et al., 2014; Hudson and Zaher, 2015; Thomas et al., 2019; Hoernes et al., 2018; Hoernes et al., 2016; You et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: O6-methylguanosine (m6G) interferes with the speed and accuracy of decoding when present in mRNA.
source: For example, our group has previously shown that O6-methylguanosine (m6G), which is highly mutagenic during DNA replication, interferes with the speed and accuracy of decoding when present in mRNA.
evidence: This is a reference to previous work by the authors' group.

claim: The effect of m6G on translation depends on its position within the codon.
source: Interestingly, the effect of m6G on translation was found to depend on its position within the codon (Hudson and Zaher, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Given the nature of the decoding process, during which three nucleotides are read simultaneously, modifications to the mRNA can have complex effects on tRNA selection that cannot be solely predicted by their effect on base pairing.
source: These observations suggest that given the nature of the decoding process, during which three nucleotides are read simultaneously, modifications to the mRNA can have complex effects on tRNA selection that cannot be solely predicted by their effect on base pairing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about m6G position-dependent effects.

claim: m1A has been found on as much as 20% of the transcriptome depending on the m1A-seq technique used.
source: Depending on the m1A-seq technique used, m1A has been found on as much as 20% of the transcriptome (Dominissini et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016), and as low as nine sites only (Safra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using different sequencing methods.

claim: Over half of the identified m1A adducts have been mapped to the coding region of transcripts.
source: Still, regardless of the method used to map the modification, over half of the identified m1A adducts have been mapped to the coding region of transcripts, suggesting that modification is likely to affect ribosome function (Dominissini et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and includes an inference about ribosome function.

claim: A specific regulatory role of m1A during translation has not been convincingly identified.
source: Notably, a specific regulatory role of this modification during translation has not been convincingly identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Studies generally support the hypothesis that m1A exists primarily as a damage adduct that disrupts the decoding process.
source: On the contrary, studies generally support the hypothesis that m1A exists primarily as a damage adduct that disrupts the decoding process (You et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of m1A at any of the three positions within the codon significantly decreased protein-synthesis yield in E. coli translation extracts.
source: This idea is supported by studies conducted using E. coli translation extracts, for which the presence of m1A at any of the three positions within the codon significantly decreased protein-synthesis yield (You et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The addition of the methyl group to the N1 atom of adenosine changes the hydrogen-bond donation and acceptance of the nucleobase.
source: This effect on translation is not unexpected, considering the structure of m1A; the addition of the methyl group to the N1 atom changes the hydrogen-bond donation and acceptance of the nucleobase.
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge about the structure of m1A.

claim: The m1A modification introduces a resonance structure with a positive charge to the nucleobase.
source: Furthermore, the modification introduces a resonance structure with a positive charge to the nucleobase.
evidence: This is based on chemical knowledge about the structure of m1A.

claim: The presence of m1A causes local duplex melting in RNA.
source: Consistent with these ideas, the presence of m1A has been shown to cause local duplex melting in RNA (Zhou et al., 2016), and hence would likely occur during codon recognition of tRNA selection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work, with an inference about codon recognition.

claim: No known methyltransferase that specifically adds m1A to mRNA has been identified.
source: No known methyltransferase that specifically adds m1A to mRNA has been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: m1A and several other adducts are hypothesized to primarily result from reactions between RNA and endogenous and exogenous chemicals.
source: Instead, m1A and several other adducts have been hypothesized to primarily result from reactions between RNA and endogenous and exogenous chemicals (Yan and Zaher, 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In yeast, the addition of alkylating compounds significantly increases the levels of m1A within mRNA, among several other adducts.
source: In yeast, for example, the addition of alkylating compounds was found to significantly increase the levels of m1A within mRNA, among several other adducts (Yan et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Alkylating compounds activate eukaryotic-quality-control pathways known to be responsible for ribosome rescue in yeast.
source: Interestingly, these compounds were also observed to activate eukaryotic-quality-control pathways known to be responsible for ribosome rescue, suggesting that alkylation stress causes ribosome stalling presumably due to its damaging effect on mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (implied from context) and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: In eukaryotes, ribosome stalling results in ribosome pileup and eventual collisions.
source: Briefly, in eukaryotes, ribosome stalling results in ribosome pileup and eventual collisions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic quality control pathways.

claim: Collided ribosomes are recognized by an E3 ligase (Hel2 in yeast and ZNF598 in mammals), which adds K63-linked ubiquitin chains to ribosomal proteins.
source: Collided ribosomes are recognized by an E3 ligase (Hel2 in yeast and ZNF598 in mammals), which adds K63-linked ubiquitin chains to ribosomal proteins (Matsuo et al., 2017; Simms et al., 2017b; Saito et al., 2015; Yan and Zaher, 2019c; Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The ubiquitination is used as a signal to recruit downstream factors involved in mRNA degradation and ribosome splitting.
source: The ubiquitination is used as a signal to recruit downstream factors involved in mRNA degradation and ribosome splitting (Matsuo et al., 2017; Ikeuchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The dissociated large-ribosome subunit, still bound to the peptidyl tRNA, is recognized by another E3 ligase (Ltn1 in yeast and listerin in mammals), which adds K48-linked ubiquitin to the nascent peptide.
source: The dissociated large-ribosome subunit, still bound to the peptidyl tRNA, is recognized by another E3 ligase (Ltn1 in yeast and listerin in mammals), which adds K48-linked ubiquitin to the nascent peptide, acting as a signal for its degradation by the proteasome (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010; Defenouillère et al., 2013; Brandman et al., 2012; Lyumkis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bacteria have evolved entirely distinct mechanisms to deal with stalled ribosomes compared to eukaryotes.
source: Bacteria appear to have evolved entirely distinct mechanisms to deal with stalled ribosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences between bacterial and eukaryotic quality control.

claim: The distinction between bacterial and eukaryotic ribosome rescue mechanisms has been hypothesized to be the result of the divergent mechanisms utilized to terminate protein synthesis and recycle the ribosome.
source: This distinction between the two domains of life has been hypothesized to be the result of the divergent mechanisms utilized to terminate protein synthesis and recycle the ribosome (Simms et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In bacteria, at least four discrete rescue mechanisms have been identified.
source: In bacteria, at least four discrete rescue mechanisms have been identified.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial ribosome rescue pathways.

claim: The tmRNA system appears to be the most widely utilized and conserved rescue pathway in bacteria.
source: Of these, the tmRNA system appears to be the most widely utilized and conserved rescue pathway (Keiler, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: tmRNA contains a transfer RNA segment, which is aminoacylated by Ala-tRNA synthetase.
source: tmRNA or transfer-messenger RNA is a unique molecule in that it contains a transfer RNA segment, which is aminoacylated by Ala-tRNA synthetase; and a messenger mRNA segment, which is used to switch the mRNA template from the defective mRNA to the molecule itself, and hence the name trans translation (Keiler et al., 1996; Moore and Sauer, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Upon ribosome stalling, tmRNA binds the A site of the ribosome in a quaternary complex with elongation factor Tu (EFTu), its partner protein SmpB and GTP.
source: Upon ribosome stalling, tmRNA binds the A site of the ribosome in a quaternary complex with elongation factor Tu (EFTu), its partner protein SmpB and GTP (Valle et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Following peptidyl transfer to tmRNA, the original defective mRNA exits the ribosome, which then begins trans translation whereby the ribosome switches template to the mRNA part of tmRNA.
source: Following peptidyl transfer to tmRNA, the original defective mRNA exits the ribosome, which then begins trans translation whereby the ribosome switches template to the mRNA part of tmRNA (Moore and Sauer, 2007; Gottesman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mRNA part of tmRNA encodes a peptide-degradation signal followed by a stop codon, ensuring that the incomplete peptide is degraded by the ClpXP protease system following canonical termination and recycling of the ribosome.
source: This mRNA encodes a peptide-degradation signal followed by a stop codon, ensuring that the incomplete peptide is degraded by the ClpXP protease system following canonical termination and recycling of the ribosome (Keiler and Sauer, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The tmRNA system has been extensively studied in the context of truncated mRNAs, which result from a myriad of conditions including ribosome stalling.
source: We note that the tmRNA system has been extensively studied in the context of truncated mRNAs, which result from a myriad of conditions including ribosome stalling (Moore and Sauer, 2007), but whether the process is also activated in response to chemical insults that modify RNA is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Whether the tmRNA process is activated in response to chemical insults that modify RNA is unknown.
source: We note that the tmRNA system has been extensively studied in the context of truncated mRNAs, which result from a myriad of conditions including ribosome stalling (Moore and Sauer, 2007), but whether the process is also activated in response to chemical insults that modify RNA is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Treating E. coli with common alkylating agents increases the levels of several potentially disruptive alkylative adducts, including m1A.
source: We first demonstrated that treating E. coli with common alkylating agents increases the levels of several potentially disruptive alkylative adducts, including m1A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: m1A reduces the rate of peptide bond formation by almost three orders of magnitude in a well-defined in vitro translation system.
source: The modification reduced the rate of peptide bond formation by almost three orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: The decrease in peptide bond formation caused by m1A is accompanied by a reduction in the endpoint of the peptidyl-transfer reaction, suggesting that the modification affects the proofreading phase of tRNA selection.
source: The decrease in peptide bond formation was also accompanied by a reduction in the endpoint of the peptidyl-transfer reaction, suggesting that the modification affects the proofreading phase of tRNA selection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Aminoglycosides, which increase peptide bond formation on mismatched-codon-anticodon interactions, have no effect on reactions with m1A-programmed mRNAs.
source: Highlighting the disruptive effect of m1A on tRNA selection was the observation that aminoglycosides, which increase peptide bond formation on mismatched-codon-anticodon interactions, had no effect on reactions with m1A-programmed mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Alkylation stress, which increases the levels of disruptive adducts such as m1A, causes widespread stalling in bacterial cells and activates rescue pathways.
source: These findings suggest that alkylation stress, which increases the levels of disruptive adducts such as m1A, causes widespread stalling in bacterial cells and activates rescue pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro and in vivo data presented.

claim: Robust activation of tmRNA occurs in E. coli cells treated with alkylating agents, even when transcription is inhibited.
source: In complete agreement with these ideas, we documented robust activation of tmRNA in E. coli cells treated with alkylating agents, even when transcription was inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: DNA damage triggers tmRNA activation, but this activation is significantly suppressed when transcription is inhibited.
source: Interestingly, DNA damage was also found to trigger tmRNA activation, but this activation was significantly suppressed when transcription was inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Alkylation stress significantly impacts translation through its effect on mRNA and rescue pathways such as trans translation are responsible for dealing with its consequences.
source: Hence, alkylation stress is likely to significantly impact translation through its effect on mRNA and rescue pathways such as trans translation are responsible for dealing with its consequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: E. coli strains lacking functional tmRNA are sensitive to alkylating agents and exhibit delayed recovery compared to wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with these proposals, E. coli strains lacking functional tmRNA were found to be sensitive to alkylating agents and exhibited delayed recovery compared to wild-type (WT) cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from growth curve analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Chemical damage to mRNA is highly detrimental to cellular homeostasis, even in organisms where mRNA is highly transient.
source: Collectively our data suggest chemical damage to mRNA is highly detrimental to cellular homeostasis, even in organisms where mRNA is highly transient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental data presented.

claim: The addition of MMS to growing yeast cultures leads to the accumulation of alkylation adducts in RNA.
source: We have recently shown that the addition of methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) to growing yeast cultures leads to the accumulation of alkylation adducts in RNA (Yan et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MMS alkylates its target through an SN2-type mechanism.
source: MMS alkylates its target through an SN2-type mechanism, while MNNG reacts through an SN1-type one (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work describing the chemical mechanisms.

claim: MNNG reacts through an SN1-type mechanism.
source: MMS alkylates its target through an SN2-type mechanism, while MNNG reacts through an SN1-type one (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work describing the chemical mechanisms.

claim: The ratio of m6A/A levels in untreated E. coli cells has been estimated to be 0.3%.
source: To confirm whether our LC-MS methods are relatively accurate, we measured the ratio of m6A/A levels in untreated cells, which has been estimated to be 0.3% in E. coli (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The measured ratio of m6A/A in untreated E. coli cells is 0.6%.
source: In agreement with these earlier studies, we measure a ratio of 0.6% (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Treatment with MMS or MNNG does not increase m6A levels in E. coli.
source: Also as expected, we did not detect an increase in m6A levels after treatment with either alkylating agent (Figure 1A), as neither MMS nor MNNG alkylate the N6 position of adenosine (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to previous work about the chemical specificity of these agents.

claim: MMS and MNNG react with N1 of G, albeit with reduced efficiency.
source: Additionally, MMS and MNNG have been shown to react with N1 of G, albeit it with reduced efficiency (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006); but we did not observe significant increases in m1G levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: m1G is a natural modification of E. coli tRNA and rRNA.
source: These observations can be rationalized by the fact that m1G is a natural modification of E. coli tRNA and rRNA (Machnicka et al., 2013), which significantly increases the background levels of the modification.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The base level of m1G is at least 200-fold higher than that of m1A.
source: Indeed, the base level of m1G is at least 200-fold higher than that of m1A (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: m7G is a natural modification in rRNA and tRNA.
source: Similarly, since m7G is a natural modification in rRNA and tRNA (Machnicka et al., 2013), we observe no significant change to its levels upon MMS and MNNG additions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with MMS or MNNG causes 10- to 200-fold increases in m3C and m1A relative levels in E. coli cells.
source: Contrary to m6A and m1G, we measured 10- to 200-fold increases in m3C and m1A relative levels in cells treated with MMS or MNNG (Figure 1D and E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Treatment with MNNG causes more than tenfold increase in m6G relative levels.
source: and a more than tenfold increase in m6G relative levels but only in those treated with MNNG (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The O6 position of guanosine is reactive with MNNG but not MMS.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that the O6 position of guanosine is reactive with MNNG but not MMS and that m3C and m1A are minor alkylative adducts in double-stranded DNA (Beranek, 1990) but are substantially more reactive as nucleophiles in the absence of hydrogen bonding (Bodell and Singer, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: m3C and m1A are minor alkylative adducts in double-stranded DNA but are substantially more reactive as nucleophiles in the absence of hydrogen bonding.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that the O6 position of guanosine is reactive with MNNG but not MMS and that m3C and m1A are minor alkylative adducts in double-stranded DNA (Beranek, 1990) but are substantially more reactive as nucleophiles in the absence of hydrogen bonding (Bodell and Singer, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: N1 of G in single-stranded RNA does not show increased reactivity because it is a secondary amine with an adjacent carbonyl group which is less reactive than N1 of A and N3 of C.
source: This same increase in reactivity for N1 to G in single-stranded RNA is not observed because it is a secondary amine with an adjacent carbonyl group which is less reactive than N1 of A and N3 of C, both of which have the higher reactivity profiles of amidine groups (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and chemical knowledge.

claim: The observed rate of peptide bond formation for the Gm1AA complex is 0.15 s−1.
source: The observed rate of 0.15 s−1 for the Gm1AA complex was measured to be more than 250-fold slower relative to the observed rate of 58 s−1 for the unmodified GAA complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed rate of peptide bond formation for the unmodified GAA complex is 58 s−1.
source: The observed rate of 0.15 s−1 for the Gm1AA complex was measured to be more than 250-fold slower relative to the observed rate of 58 s−1 for the unmodified GAA complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The endpoint of the m1A reaction is approximately tenfold lower relative to the unmodified reaction.
source: Furthermore, the endpoint of the m1A reaction, which reports on the efficiency of proofreading (Pape et al., 1999), was found to be ~tenfold lower relative to the unmodified one (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citation about what the endpoint represents.

claim: m1A is highly detrimental to the tRNA selection process and is highly likely to stall ribosomes in vivo.
source: These results demonstrate that m1A is highly detrimental to the tRNA selection process and is highly likely to stall ribosomes in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro experimental data.

claim: During tRNA selection, aa-tRNAs that have only one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon are termed near-cognate.
source: During tRNA selection, aa-tRNAs that have only one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon are termed near-cognate (Gromadski and Rodnina, 2004a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The addition of certain aminoglycosides alters the selection process and allows for the misincorporation of near-cognate aa-tRNAs.
source: Although the ribosome efficiently discriminates against the incorporation of near-cognate aa-tRNAs, the addition of certain aminoglycosides alters the selection process and allows for their misincorporation (Pape et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Paromomycin binds the decoding center of the ribosome, which leads to local conformational changes that lower the energy barrier required to shift the ribosome into a 'closed' conformation.
source: For instance, paromomycin binds the decoding center of the ribosome, which leads to local conformational changes that lower the energy barrier required to shift the ribosome into a 'closed' conformation (Fourmy et al., 1996; Ogle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The closed conformation typically occurs in the presence of cognate aa-tRNAs and is a prerequisite for their accommodation into the active site of the ribosome for peptidyl transfer to take place.
source: This conformation typically occurs in the presence of cognate aa-tRNAs and is a prerequisite for their accommodation into the active site of the ribosome for peptidyl transfer to take place (Ogle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The addition of aminoglycosides to reactions containing non-cognate aa-tRNAs has little to no effect on peptide bond formation.
source: By contrast, the addition of aminoglycosides to reactions containing non-cognate aa-tRNAs, which harbor more than one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon, has little to no effect on peptide bond formation (Pape et al., 2000; Gromadski and Rodnina, 2004b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The addition of paromomycin and streptomycin de-represses the effects of the oxidative adduct 8-oxoguanosine (8-oxoG) on peptide bond formation.
source: For instance, we recently showed that the addition of paromomycin and streptomycin de-represses the effects of the oxidative adduct 8-oxoguanosine (8-oxoG) on peptide bond formation (Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The ribosome recognizes 8-oxoG as a simple mismatch when paired with its partner nucleotide.
source: These findings suggest that the ribosome recognizes this modification as a simple mismatch when paired with its partner nucleotide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of aminoglycosides on 8-oxoG.

claim: In the presence of m1A, the addition of paromomycin has little to no effect on the observed rate of peptide bond formation.
source: Interestingly and in contrast to 8-oxoG, in the presence of m1A, we found the addition of paromomycin to have little to no effect on the observed rate of peptide bond formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observed rate of peptide bond formation in the presence of m1A is 0.15 s−1 without paromomycin and 0.2 s−1 with paromomycin.
source: In particular, we measured observed rates of 0.15 s−1 and 0.2 s−1 in the absence and presence of an antibiotic, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The endpoints of reactions with m1A are 0.10 without paromomycin and 0.11 with paromomycin.
source: Additionally, the endpoints of the very same reactions were 0.10 and 0.11, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the same experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: m1A is unable to base pair with U in the decoding center and significantly distorts the codon-anticodon helix.
source: These findings suggest that not only is m1A unable to base pair with U in the decoding center but that the modification significantly distorts the codon-anticodon helix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of paromomycin on m1A-containing reactions.

claim: The distortion caused by m1A results in the aa-tRNA, that is otherwise cognate, to be recognized as a non-cognate one by the ribosome.
source: This distortion results in the aa-tRNA, that is otherwise cognate, to be recognized as a non-cognate one by the ribosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of paromomycin on m1A-containing reactions.

claim: For the codon containing unmodified adenosine, no significant dipeptide accumulation occurs except in the presence of the cognate Glu-tRNAGlu ternary complex.
source: As anticipated, for the codon containing the unmodified adenosine, we observed no significant dipeptide accumulation except in the presence of the cognate Glu-tRNAGlu ternary complex (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the codon containing m1A, no significant dipeptide accumulation occurs in the presence of any aa-tRNA.
source: For the codon containing m1A, no significant dipeptide accumulation occurred in the presence of any aa-tRNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The m1A modification inhibits base pairing altogether and does not alter the base-pairing preference of the nucleotide.
source: These findings strongly suggest that the modification inhibits base pairing altogether and does not alter the base-pairing preference of the nucleotide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the aa-tRNA reactivity survey data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two- to threefold increases in His6-tagging levels occur upon the addition of MMS and MNNG to E. coli expressing tmRNA-His6.
source: Consistent with our proposal that alkylation stress activates the tmRNA system, we observed two- to threefold increases in His6-tagging levels upon the addition of MMS and MNNG to E. coli expressing tmRNA-His6 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The increase in tmRNA activity upon alkylation stress is accompanied by activation of the adaptive response as judged by the accumulation of Ada protein.
source: As expected, this increase in tmRNA activity was accompanied by activation of the adaptive response as judged by the accumulation of Ada protein, the principal mediator of the process in response to alkylation damage (Jeggo, 1979; Sakumi and Sekiguchi, 1989; Uphoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claim: Activation of the SOS response occurs upon alkylation stress as evaluated by the accumulation of RecA.
source: We also observe activation of the SOS response as evaluated by the accumulation of its principal mediator RecA (Cox, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to previous work.

claim: At 0.1% MMS concentration and 20 min treatment duration, there is little to no effect on cellular viability.
source: It is worth noting that at this concentration of MMS and duration of treatment, we observe little to no effect on cellular viability as assessed by spot assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Under normal conditions, His-tagged products resulting from tmRNA activation are targeted for degradation by the ClpAP, ClpXP, and Lon proteases.
source: Under normal conditions, His-tagged products resulting from tmRNA activation are targeted for degradation by the ClpAP, ClpXP, and Lon proteases, presumably because they are incomplete peptides that are likely to misfold.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fate of tmRNA-tagged proteins.

claim: Previous reports have shown the deletion of ΔclpP, clpX, and lon genes to result in increased accumulation of His-tagged products.
source: Indeed, previous reports have shown the deletion of ΔclpP, clpX, and lon genes to result in increased accumulation of His-tagged products (Moore and Sauer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The levels of His-tagging triggered by the addition of alkylation compounds increased by more than twofold in the absence of ClpP, ClpX, and Lon proteases.
source: As expected, the levels of His-tagging triggered by the addition of alkylation compounds increased by more than twofold in the absence of these proteases (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In clpP, clpX, and lon cells, Ada accumulates even in the absence of alkylation stress.
source: In agreement with previous studies that suggested Ada is subject to proteolysis (Sedgwick, 1989), in clpP, clpX, and lon cells, the factor was observed to accumulate even in the absence of alkylation stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: The observed consistent His-tagging pattern is likely due to an artifact of the His antibodies rather than a particular subset of proteins that are preferentially His-tagged at certain locations.
source: Thus, the observed consistent His-tagging pattern is likely due to an artifact of the His antibodies rather than a particular subset of proteins that are preferentially His-tagged at certain locations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different antibodies produce different patterns (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: Pretreatment with rifampicin only slightly decreased the amount of His-tagging induced by MMS and MNNG (10–20%).
source: In agreement with our model, pretreatment with rifampicin only slightly decreased the amount of His-tagging induced by MMS and MNNG (10–20%) (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The majority of the observed tmRNA activity in response to MMS and MNNG is due to direct damage to the mRNA.
source: suggesting that the majority of the observed tmRNA activity is due to direct damage to the mRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rifampicin pretreatment data.

claim: Rifampicin pretreatment combined with ciprofloxacin treatment decreased the amount of His-tagging by almost twofold.
source: In contrast, the same rifampicin pretreatment combined with ciprofloxacin treatment decreased the amount of His-tagging by almost twofold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For mitomycin C treatment, no His-tagging was observed even though significant DNA damage had occurred as assessed by the increase in RecA levels.
source: Interestingly, for the mitomycin C treatment, we did not observe any His-tagging even though we could infer that significant DNA damage had occurred as assessed by the increase in RecA levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: While truncated transcripts produced from damaged DNA do activate tmRNA, the predominant trigger of tmRNA activation in MMS- and MNNG-treated samples is alkylative damage of RNA.
source: Regardless of this last observation, we conclude that while truncated transcripts produced from damaged DNA do activate tmRNA, the predominant trigger of tmRNA activation in MMS- and MNNG-treated samples is alkylative damage of RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rifampicin pretreatment experiments.

claim: Both mock-treated and MMS-treated mRNA were translated efficiently in S30 extracts, with the MMS-treated mRNA yielding slightly less full-length product.
source: 35S labeling and western-blotting analysis (using anti-FLAG antibody) revealed that both mRNA species were translated efficiently in our extract, with the MMS-treated mRNA yielding slightly less full-length product.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Modification by MMS results in stalling on mRNA in cell-free translation systems.
source: These observations suggest that modification by MMS results in stalling on this mRNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced full-length product from MMS-treated mRNA.

claim: tmRNA is significantly activated in reactions containing damaged mRNA in cell-free translation systems.
source: Notably, probing with anti-His antibody revealed that tmRNA is significantly activated in reactions containing damaged mRNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: tmRNA tagging occurs on modified mRNA in a system where transcription is not occurring.
source: The observation that tmRNA tagging occurs on modified mRNA in a system where transcription is not occurring provides important support for our model that trans translation responds to ribosome stalling on damaged mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the cell-free translation system shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In addition to trans translation, tmRNA plays a role in the degradation of its target mRNAs.
source: Previous studies indicated that in addition to trans translation, tmRNA plays a role in the degradation of its target mRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the context of previous studies.

claim: tmRNA facilitates the recruitment of RNase R, which initiates nonstop mRNA decay.
source: In particular, the molecule facilitates the recruitment of RNase R, which initiates nonstop mRNA decay (Ge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Deletion of the ssrA gene results in the accumulation of nonstop mRNAs.
source: As our findings suggest that ribosomes stalled on modified mRNAs engage the trans-translation machinery, we hypothesized that tmRNA is also likely to play a role in the degradation of chemically damaged mRNAs. We note that analogous studies by our group conducted in yeast took advantage of the polyA tail of mRNAs in eukaryotes in order to purify them before modification analysis by LC-MS (Yan et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of tmRNA in mRNA degradation.

claim: Treating cells with MMS causes a significant increase in the m6A signal for RNA species that co-migrated between rRNA and tRNA species after base treatment.
source: By contrast, base treatment of the gel before transfer revealed that treating cells with MMS causes a significant increase in the signal for RNA species that co-migrated between rRNA and tRNA species, which we attribute to mRNA species having m1A modification (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The MMS-induced m6A signal (from converted m1A) is much higher in the ΔssrA cells.
source: More important was the observation that the MMS-induced signal was much higher in the ΔssrA cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tmRNA rescues ribosomes stalled on modified mRNAs and m1A levels in mRNA increase in its absence.
source: Our observations suggest that not only does tmRNA rescue ribosomes stalled on modified mRNAs, but that m1A levels in mRNA increase in its absence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoblotting data showing higher m1A-derived signal in ΔssrA cells.

claim: Previous studies have shown that ∆ssrA E. coli strains show no appreciable growth phenotype under standard laboratory conditions but do exhibit delayed growth under certain stress conditions.
source: Even though the ssrA gene that encodes tmRNA is highly conserved in bacteria, previous studies have shown that ∆ssrA E. coli strains show no appreciable growth phenotype under standard laboratory conditions but do exhibit delayed growth under certain stress conditions (Nishikawa et al., 2006; Karzai et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: After treatment with MMS or MNNG, ∆ssrA cells have an approximately 1.5 hr lag in their recovery compared to WT cells.
source: However, after treatment with MMS or MNNG, ∆ssrA cells have an approximately 1.5 hr lag in their recovery compared to WT cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Similar levels of cell death occur for ∆ssrA and WT cells after treatment with 0.5% MMS.
source: We observe similar levels of cell death for ∆ssrA and WT cells, suggesting that the observed lag in recovery time is not due to a difference in the number of cells killed, but rather the ability of the cells to quickly recover after treatment with alkylating agents (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The observed lag in recovery time for ∆ssrA cells is not due to a difference in the number of cells killed, but rather the ability of the cells to quickly recover after treatment with alkylating agents.
source: We observe similar levels of cell death for ∆ssrA and WT cells, suggesting that the observed lag in recovery time is not due to a difference in the number of cells killed, but rather the ability of the cells to quickly recover after treatment with alkylating agents (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the viability data.

claim: Cells employ trans translation to rescue ribosomes stalled on damaged mRNA to quickly recover from alkylation stress.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that cells employ trans translation to rescue ribosomes stalled on damaged mRNA to quickly recover from alkylation stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental data showing delayed recovery in ∆ssrA cells.

claim: m6A is arguably one of the most significant enzymatic modifications to mRNA and appears to play important roles in the regulation of gene expression.
source: Among these modifications, m6A is arguably one of the most significant ones and appears to play important roles in the regulation of gene expression (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pseudouridine-modified mRNAs are less immunogenic and produce significantly higher levels of functional proteins than their unmodified counterpart.
source: Interestingly, pseudouridine-modified (and derivatives of Ψ) mRNAs have been shown to be effective for biotechnological purposes as they are less immunogenic and produce significantly higher levels of functional proteins than their unmodified counterpart (Karikó et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Most chemical modifications of mRNA are disruptive damage adducts.
source: Although much has been revealed about the role the so-called intentional modifications serve in regulating various aspects of mRNA metabolism, most chemical modifications of mRNA are disruptive damage adducts (Simms and Zaher, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Several alkylative damage adducts, including m1A and m6G, drastically slow translation and increase miscoding in vitro.
source: Previous work had shown that several alkylative damage adducts, including m1A and m6G, drastically slow translation and increase miscoding in vitro (Hudson and Zaher, 2015; You et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Little is known about how alkylative damage of mRNA elicits cellular responses in vivo, especially in bacteria.
source: However, little is known about how alkylative damage of mRNA elicits cellular responses in vivo, and especially in bacteria.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The response to alkylation-mediated changes to translation is likely to be general, as it was nearly identical regardless of the specific compound used to elicit the damage.
source: This response to alkylation-mediated changes to translation is likely to be general, as it was nearly identical regardless of the specific compound used to elicit the damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar responses observed with MMS and MNNG.

claim: The addition of MNNG leads to a more than tenfold increase in m6G levels, whereas that of MMS leads to a modest <1.5-fold increase for the same modification.
source: For instance, the addition of MNNG leads to a more than tenfold increase in m6G levels, whereas that of MMS leads to a modest <1.5-fold increase for the same modification (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: MNNG produces a greater percentage of O-methyl adducts than MMS.
source: This is consistent with studies showing that MNNG produces a greater percentage of O-methyl adducts (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The modification by m1A severely inhibits tRNA selection by the ribosome as reflected by the three orders of magnitude drop in the observed rate of peptide bond formation and the tenfold decrease in the endpoint of the reaction.
source: As expected, the modification severely inhibited tRNA selection by the ribosome as reflected by the three orders of magnitude drop in the observed rate of peptide bond formation and the tenfold decrease in the endpoint of the reaction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: m1A in mRNA significantly decreased protein-synthesis yield in S30 extracts.
source: This is consistent with a previous study showing that m1A in mRNA significantly decreased protein-synthesis yield in S30 extracts (You et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The addition of paromomycin does not suppress the inhibitory effect of m1A on peptide bond formation.
source: Interestingly, while the observation that m1A severely inhibits decoding is expected, our finding that the addition of paromomycin does not suppress this effect at all (Figure 3) is unanticipated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The m1A modification is so disruptive that it affects base-pairing between the neighboring nucleotides.
source: Since paromomycin allows the incorporation of near-cognate aa-tRNAs (Pape et al., 2000; i.e. those that have one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon), this observation suggests that the modification is so disruptive that it affects base-pairing between the neighboring nucleotides.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of paromomycin effect and citation to previous work.

claim: All aa-tRNAs are recognized as non cognates in the presence of m1A.
source: Consequently, all aa-tRNAs are recognized as non cognates, or as having more than one mismatch (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the aa-tRNA reactivity survey shown in Figure 4.

claim: A significant increase in His-tagging and hence increased trans-translation activity occurs upon cellular treatment with alkylating agents.
source: In complete agreement with our model, we observe a significant increase in His-tagging and hence increased trans-translation activity upon cellular treatment with alkylating agents (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: tmRNA activity is independent of active transcription.
source: We also showed that this activity is independent of active transcription (Figure 5)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from rifampicin pretreatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: tmRNA activity in response to alkylation stress is likely to be initiated as a result of direct damage to mature mRNAs.
source: and hence is likely to be initiated as a result of direct damage to mature mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rifampicin pretreatment data.

claim: Bacterial mRNAs do not contain poly-A tails like their eukaryotic counterparts.
source: Notably, because bacterial mRNAs do not contain poly-A tails like their eukaryotic counterparts, it is difficult to purify mRNA away from rRNA and tRNA
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural differences between bacterial and eukaryotic mRNAs.

claim: Trans translation has been studied almost exclusively in the context of defective mRNAs.
source: For one, trans translation has been studied almost exclusively in the context of defective mRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the focus of previous tmRNA research.

claim: The folding of rRNA as well as its association with ribosomal proteins makes it a poor target for alkylative damage.
source: Second, the folding of rRNA as well as its association with ribosomal proteins is thought to make it a poor target for alkylative damage (Simms and Zaher, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The rRNA residues responsible for monitoring the base pairing in the decoding center are not exposed and unlikely to be damaged by alkylating agents at a high incidence.
source: Specifically, the rRNA residues responsible for monitoring the base pairing in the decoding center are not exposed; therefore, it is unlikely that they are damaged by the agents at a high incidence (Clemons et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: Only 3 out of an average of 76 nucleotides in tRNAs directly participate in base pairing with the codon.
source: Additionally, tRNAs are susceptible to alkylative damage, but only 3 out of an average of 76 nucleotides directly participate in base pairing with the codon.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of tRNA structure and function.

claim: The CCA-adding enzyme in E. coli discriminates against tRNA backbone damage.
source: Finally, the CCA-adding enzyme in E. coli has been shown to discriminate against tRNA backbone damage (Hou, 2010); without CCA ends these tRNAs are not aminoacylated and cannot participate in peptidyl transfer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bacteria lacking a functional trans-translation pathway do not recover as efficiently after cellular stress, including metabolic and oxidative stress.
source: Several studies have shown that bacteria lacking a functional trans-translation pathway do not recover as efficiently after cellular stress, including metabolic and oxidative stress (Nishikawa et al., 2006; Karzai et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Alkylative stress causes a delayed recovery period in cells lacking tmRNA, likely because they are unable to efficiently rescue stalled ribosomes and resume growth.
source: We observe that alkylative stress also causes a delayed recovery period in cells lacking tmRNA, likely because they are unable to efficiently rescue stalled ribosomes and resume growth (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Alternative ribosome-rescue factor A (ArfA) works by recruiting RF2 to hydrolyze the peptidyl-tRNA and release the ribosome.
source: One factor, known as alternative ribosome-rescue factor A (ArfA) works by recruiting RF2 to hydrolyze the peptidyl-tRNA and release the ribosome (Shimizu, 2012; Chadani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ArfA acts as a backup for trans-translation, as its expression increases when tmRNA activity is limited.
source: This factor acts as a backup for trans-translation, as its expression increases when tmRNA activity is limited (Garza-Sánchez et al., 2011; Chadani et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ArfB can release stalled ribosomes, although it does not appear to function solely as a backup for tmRNA and its physiological function remains to be elucidated.
source: Another factor that can release stalled ribosomes is ArfB, although it does not appear to function solely as a backup for tmRNA and its physiological function remains to be elucidated (Chadani et al., 2011b; Handa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Alternative ribosome rescue factors in E. coli are likely responsible for the eventual recovery observed in ∆ssrA cells.
source: Regardless, these alternative ribosome rescue factors in E. coli are likely responsible for the eventual recovery we observe
evidence: This is an inference based on the knowledge of alternative rescue pathways and the observed recovery of ∆ssrA cells.
